lessons.title: Reading the Payoff: Hedged vs Unhedged Positions at Expiry

children.text: Open any options app and it will happily draw you a payoff diagram. The problem is that it draws the option on its own: a hockey stick that makes a ₹250 put look like a lottery ticket. That is the speculator's picture. A hedger needs a different picture, one that adds the option to the portfolio it protects. This lesson teaches you to build that combined diagram yourself and read four things off it in seconds: the floor, the kink, the slope and the breakeven. It also shows you what the neat expiry-day diagram hides about the weeks before expiry, which is exactly when most investors panic that their hedge is not working.

body.text: To read a hedge, add the lines. The portfolio line plus the option line gives the only diagram that matters, and its shape tells you your floor, where protection starts, how much of each move you still carry, and where you break even.

children.text: Building the Combined Diagram in Three Steps

Use the familiar setup: the Nifty at 25,000, a Nifty-tracking portfolio, and a three-month 24,000 put bought at ₹250. Work per unit of the Nifty first, then multiply by the lot size at the end. Per-unit numbers keep the shapes clear.
Draw the portfolio line.
Profit or loss per unit = Nifty at expiry − 25,000. A straight diagonal line: every point the Nifty moves, you move one point.
Draw the option line.
Profit or loss per unit = max(24,000 − Nifty at expiry, 0) − 250. Flat at −250 above the strike, rising one point for every point the Nifty falls below it.
Add them at each price.
Pick a range of expiry levels, add the two numbers, and plot the result.

body.caption: Step 2 on its own: the 24,000 put, per unit. This is what your broker app shows. On its own it tells you almost nothing about your portfolio.
Step 3: adding the lines, per unit of the Nifty

children.text: Four Things to Read Off Any Hedge Diagram

cells: Height of the flat section on the left
Your worst case at expiry, no matter how far the market falls
The level below which the protection takes over
How much of each market move you still carry in that zone
How far the market must rise to recover the premium

body.text: Slope is the most underrated feature. A slope of 1 means you carry every point of the move, good or bad. A slope of 0 means the market can move and your position does not. A full hedge gives you slope 1 above the strike and 0 below it. That asymmetry, full participation on the way up and none on the way down past the floor, is precisely what the premium buys.

body.title: Find the kink
body.textWithBlank: On the combined diagram of a portfolio plus a protective put, the line bends at the put's ___ price.
body.explanation: Above the strike, the put is worthless at expiry and the combined line follows the portfolio. Below it, the put gains point for point, so the line goes flat. The change happens exactly at the strike.

children.text: Partial Hedges Change the Slope, Not the Kink

Return to the ₹32,50,000 portfolio from the last lesson, which is two lots or 130 units. With one lot of puts it is 50% hedged, with two lots 100%. Draw all three in rupees and something useful appears. The kink stays at 24,000 in every case. What changes is the slope below it. A 50% hedge leaves the line tilted at half the unhedged steepness, so there is no true floor, just a slower fall.

body.caption: 0% hedged: slope 1. 50% hedged: slope 0.5. 100% hedged: slope 0, a true floor.

body.title: ₹32.5 lakh portfolio at expiry: 0%, 50% and 100% hedged with 24,000 puts
Read the slope
body.question: On the 50% hedged line, the Nifty falls from 23,000 to 22,000 at expiry. How much does the combined position change, and why?
options: Nothing, because the position is below the strike and protected
About ₹65,000, because half the exposure is still unprotected
About ₹1,30,000, because a partial hedge gives no protection
body.explanation: A 1,000-point fall costs the 130-unit portfolio ₹1,30,000. The single lot of puts gains 1,000 × 65 = ₹65,000. Net change: −₹65,000. The chart confirms it: −2.11 lakh to −2.76 lakh. Slope 0.5 means you carry half of every point below the strike.

body.title: Read a point off the 50% line
body.prompt: For the ₹32,50,000 portfolio (130 units) with one lot (65 units) of the 24,000 put bought at ₹250, what is the combined loss if the Nifty is at 22,500 at expiry? Enter the loss as a positive number in rupees.

children.text: What the Expiry Diagram Hides: The Weeks Before

markDefs.definition: How much an option's price changes for a one-point move in the underlying. A put with a delta of −0.42 gains about 42 paise for every rupee the underlying falls.

children.text: Every diagram so far shows expiry day, when the put is worth exactly its intrinsic value. Before expiry, the put still carries time value, and its price does not move point for point with the Nifty. How much it moves is its
delta
. So one month into a three-month hedge, the combined line is not a sharp hockey stick. It is a smooth curve.

body.caption: The same hedge one month in, with two months left (illustrative put values, volatility rising as the market falls)
headers: Combined per unit, one month in

body.title: Combined hedge per unit: one month in vs at expiry

children.text: Three lessons sit in that chart:
Near the strike, you are better off than the expiry line.
At 24,000 one month in, the put still has ₹520 of value, so the combined loss is 730 points, not 1,250. The remaining time value is worth something if you sell the put now.
Protection builds gradually, not all at once.

With the Nifty still at 25,000, the put offsets only about 19% of the next move. At 24,000 it offsets about 42%. The flat floor you see on the expiry diagram only fully appears as expiry approaches or the market falls deep below the strike.
Deep below the strike, the floor can sag slightly before expiry.

At 22,000 the put is worth ₹1,894, a little below its ₹2,000 intrinsic value, because NSE options are European and money received later is worth slightly less today. Hold to expiry and the full floor is restored.

body.title: "My hedge isn't working"
body.scenario: Deepa, 50, a pharmacist in Nagpur, holds ₹16,25,000 in a Nifty 50 index fund. With the Nifty at 25,000, she buys one lot of the three-month 24,000 put at ₹250 (₹16,250). Four weeks later, the Nifty has fallen to 24,000. Her fund is down ₹65,000. She checks her put and sees it is worth ₹520, a gain of only ₹17,550. "I paid for insurance and I'm still down ₹47,450," she messages her brother. "The hedge is useless."
body.prompt: Is Deepa right? Explain what is actually happening, and what her worst case still is if she holds the put to expiry.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The hedge is working exactly as designed. The Nifty has only just reached the 24,000 strike. The first 4% of the fall was always her deductible, and she knew it when she chose that strike.
2. Her combined loss one month in is ₹65,000 − ₹17,550 = ₹47,450. At expiry, at the same Nifty level, it would be ₹81,250, because the put's remaining time value would have decayed. Right now she is actually ahead of her expiry-day number.
3. The put's delta is now around −0.42, so it offsets roughly 42% of any further fall today, and that share rises the further the market drops.
4. Her worst case is unchanged. If she holds the put to expiry, her maximum loss is ₹81,250, about 5%, however far the Nifty falls.
5. The mistake is judging the hedge against the expiry diagram before expiry, or against the put's own profit instead of the whole portfolio. Selling the put now in frustration would remove her floor just as the market is testing it.

body.text: A payoff diagram does not show probability, timing, taxes, transaction costs, or how closely your real portfolio tracks the index. It shows what happens at each price if everything else goes to plan. Use it to understand the shape of your risk, never as a forecast.

body.title: Why a protective put looks exactly like a call

children.text: Look at the combined hedged line again: flat on the left, rising on the right, kinked at 24,000. That is the shape of a long call with a 24,000 strike. It is not a coincidence. Owning the index plus a put has the same payoff shape as owning a call plus keeping the strike amount in cash, a relationship called put-call parity.

content.caption: A three-month 24,000 call at an illustrative ₹1,640, per unit. Compare its shape with the combined hedged line above.

children.text: Below the strike, the call loses 1,640 points while the hedged portfolio loses 1,250. The 390-point difference is roughly the interest on ₹24,000 for three months at 6.5% (24,000 × 0.065 × 0.25 = 390), which the call buyer earns by keeping cash instead of holding the index. For a long-term investor this matters little in practice, but it shows that a fully hedged portfolio behaves like an option position, not like a normal equity holding.

body.title: Draw your own hedge diagram
steps: Pick seven index levels at expiry, from about 15% below today's level to 10% above it.
For each level, calculate your portfolio's profit or loss in rupees.
For each level, calculate the puts' payoff minus premium, multiplied by the number of units.
Add the two columns and plot the result, by hand or in a spreadsheet.
Mark the floor, kink, slope below the strike and breakeven, and check that each matches what you intended.

cards.definition: Portfolio profit or loss plus option profit or loss at each price. The only diagram that shows a hedge properly.
The flat section on the left of a fully hedged diagram. Your worst case at expiry.
The point where the combined line changes direction, at the put's strike.
How much of each market move you carry. Below the strike, slope = 1 − hedge ratio.
How much an option's price moves per point of the underlying before expiry. It explains why protection builds gradually.
The relationship showing that index plus put has the same payoff shape as a call plus cash.

points: Broker apps show the option alone. A hedger must add the portfolio line to see the real position.
Read four features: floor, kink (at the strike), slope in each zone, and breakeven (starting level plus premium).
A partial hedge keeps the kink but leaves a slope of 1 − hedge ratio below the strike, so there is no true floor.
Expiry diagrams are exact only on expiry day. Before that, the combined line is a smooth curve and protection builds with delta.
Judging a hedge mid-term against its expiry diagram leads investors to abandon it just when it starts to matter.
A payoff diagram shows shape, not probability, costs, taxes or tracking error.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Option values, deltas and premiums are illustrative estimates from a standard pricing model, and real market prices will differ. Examples assume the portfolio moves exactly with the Nifty 50. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before using options.
